lessons.title: Hindi Basics and Greetings 🙏
lessons.description: Learn essential Hindi greetings, polite expressions, and the fundamental distinction between formal and informal address, including both male and female grammatical forms.
objectives: Master standard daily greetings in Hindi
Understand when to use formal ('Aap') vs informal ('Tum') address
Express gratitude, apologies, and farewells correctly
Recognize both male and female verb agreements in basic responses
lessons.explanation: In spoken Hindi, greetings set the tone for all social and professional interactions. The most universal greeting is 'Namaste' (नमस्ते), which is used at any time of day and is suitable for both formal and informal settings. When addressing elders, seniors, or people you are meeting for the first time, you must use the formal pronoun 'Aap' (आप). As you build rapport, you may use 'Tum' (तुम) with peers or younger individuals. Polite expressions like 'Dhanyawad' (धन्यवाद) for thank you and 'Maaf kijiye' (माफ़ कीजिए) for excuse me or sorry are crucial for smooth everyday communication.

dialogue.meaning: Yes, everything is fixed. See you again!

commonMistakes.explanation: Mixing pronouns ('Tum') with formal verb endings ('hain') is incorrect. Use 'Tum kaise ho?' or 'Tum kaisi ho?' for informal address.
Adding 'ji' to 'Dhanyawad' is unnatural in spoken Hindi. Simply say 'Dhanyawad' or 'Shukriya'.
When speaking formally to superiors or professionals, use the polite imperative form 'Maaf kijiye' instead of the blunt 'Maaf karo'.

lessons.title: Introducing Yourself 🤝
lessons.description: Learn how to state your name, where you are from, your profession, and ask basic introductory questions using both male and female grammatical patterns.
objectives: State your full name naturally in Hindi
Explain where you live or are from using correct gender markers ('ka' for male, 'ki' for female)
Describe your profession using both masculine and feminine forms
Ask someone else their name and background
lessons.explanation: Introducing yourself in spoken Hindi relies on simple sentence patterns. To state your name, use 'Mera naam [Name] hai' (My name is [Name]). To state your origin, male speakers use 'Main [City] ka hoon' while female speakers use 'Main [City] ki hoon'. For professions, use 'Main ek [Profession] hoon'. When asking someone else their name politely, you say 'Aapka naam kya hai?' (What is your name?).

lessons.title: Personal Pronouns 🙋🏻‍♂️🙋🏻‍♀️
lessons.description: Master personal pronouns in Hindi (I, you, he, she, we, they) and understand formal versus informal distinctions for both genders.
objectives: Learn all primary personal pronouns in Hindi
Understand the three levels of 'you' (Aap, Tum, Tu)
Distinguish between proximate and distant third-person pronouns (Yeh/Vah)
Pair pronouns correctly with basic verbs across gender agreements
lessons.explanation:
Pronouns are the building blocks of sentence formation. In Hindi, personal pronouns change depending on the level of formality and social distance. 
- 'Main' = I
- 'Aap' = You (Formal / Respectful, used for elders, colleagues, strangers)
- 'Tum' = You (Informal / Peer, used for friends, younger people)
- 'Tu' = You (Very intimate / Casual, avoid in professional settings)
- 'Yeh' = This / He / She (Close proximity)
- 'Vah' = That / He / She (Distant proximity)
- 'Hum' = We
- 'Ve' / 'Ye' = They / These / Those
Verbs like 'hoon' (am), 'hain' (are/is-formal), and 'ho' (are-informal) agree directly with these pronouns.

lessons.title: Everyday Expressions 📆
lessons.description: Learn common phrases for agreement, disagreement, expressing lack of understanding, and managing daily social cues for all speakers.
objectives: Express agreement ('Theek hai', 'Sahi hai') and disagreement
Indicate understanding ('Samjh gaya/gayi') or confusion
Ask someone to repeat or speak slowly
Manage polite conversational transitions
lessons.explanation: In fast-paced conversations, relying solely on textbook sentences can feel rigid. Spoken Hindi makes heavy use of conversational fillers and reaction expressions. Phrases like 'Theek hai' (Okay/Fine), 'Sahi hai' (That's correct), 'Samjh gaya' (I understood - male) or 'Samjh gayi' (I understood - female), and 'Mujhe maloom nahi' (I don't know) allow you to participate actively even with a limited vocabulary.

lessons.title: Asking Basic Questions 🤔❓
lessons.description: Learn the primary WH-question words in Hindi (What, Where, When, Who, Why, How) and how to construct basic inquiries for all learners.
objectives: Master the 6 core WH-question words in Hindi
Construct simple direct questions for daily situations
Understand question word placement in spoken Hindi
Ask for identification, location, time, and reason
lessons.explanation:
To converse effectively, you must be able to ask questions. In Hindi, question words generally appear right before the verb or at the natural emphasis point of the sentence. 
- 'Kya' = What
- 'Kahan' = Where
- 'Kaun' = Who
- 'Kab' = When
- 'Kyun' = Why
- 'Kaise' = How
Additionally, starting a sentence with 'Kya' converts a statement into a Yes/No question.

lessons.explanation: Verbs are action words that bring sentences to life. In Hindi, dictionary-form verbs always end with the syllable '-na' (जैसे - jana, khana). To use a verb in spoken Hindi, you drop the '-na' to get the root form and add appropriate gender and number endings based on who is doing the action.

lessons.title: Family and Friends 👨‍👩‍👧‍👦

lessons.explanation: Indian culture places high value on family relationships. Hindi has distinct terms for paternal and maternal relatives, as well as elder versus younger siblings. For everyday conversation, key core terms include 'Mata ji' (Mother), 'Pita ji' (Father), 'Bhai' (Brother), 'Behen' (Sister), and 'Dost' (Friend). Adding 'ji' after titles or names shows respect.

lessons.explanation: In Hindi, simple past tense is formed by dropping the infinitive verb ending '-na' from the root and adding past tense markers based on the gender and number of the subject. lessons.title: Present Tense ⏳
lessons.description: Master Present Simple and Present Continuous tenses in Hindi with dual-gender markers for daily routines and current actions.
objectives: Form Present Habitual/Simple sentences ('ta hoon' / 'ti hoon')
Form Present Continuous sentences ('raha hoon' / 'rahi hoon')
Distinguish clearly between routine actions and ongoing actions
Apply correct masculine and feminine verb endings in present tense
lessons.explanation:
Present Tense has two major forms in daily conversation:
1. Present Habitual / Routine (I do / I eat):
   - Male speaker: Root + ta hoon (e.g., Main jata hoon)
   - Female speaker: Root + ti hoon (e.g., Main jaati hoon)
2. Present Continuous (I am doing / I am going):
   - Male speaker: Root + raha hoon (e.g., Main ja raha hoon)
   - Female speaker: Root + rahi hoon (e.g., Main ja rahi hoon)
For formal address ('Aap'), use 'te hain' (male) / 'ti hain' (female) for routine, and 'rahe hain' / 'rahi hain' for continuous actions.

lessons.title: Future Tense 🚀
lessons.description: Master future tense in Hindi to express upcoming actions, plans, intentions, and promises with proper verb agreements.
objectives: Form simple future tense statements ('ga / gi / ge')
Express future plans, appointments, and commitments
Match future tense verb suffixes with pronouns and gender
Use future time markers like 'kal' (tomorrow)
lessons.explanation:
Future tense in Hindi is formed by taking the verb root and adding suffixes that depend on the subject's gender and person: 
- For 'Main' (I): add '-unga' (male) or '-ungi' (female) (e.g., jaunga / jaungi).
- For 'Aap' (You formal) / 'Ve' (They) / 'Hum' (We): add '-enge' (male/mixed) or '-engi' (female plural) (e.g., jaenge).
- For singular third-person ('Vah' he/she): add '-ega' (male) or '-egi' (female) (e.g., jaega / jaegi).
